memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Isn't this the cup my master drinks from and also uses for divination? This is a wicked thing you have done." — Gen 44:5 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The mention of divination surprises many readers. Does this mean Joseph practised it? The text does not actually say he did. Joseph is playing the role of an Egyptian official, and this is exactly the sort of thing such an official would say — and later he will tell his brothers plainly that God, not a cup, revealed things to him (Gen 41:16). The steward speaks the language his audience would expect. Scripture records the words honestly without endorsing them; the Bible is clear elsewhere that divination is forbidden (Deut 18:10-12).

What the verse really wants us to feel is the weight of the charge. "This is a wicked thing you have done." The brothers are being told they have committed a serious crime against a man who showed them nothing but kindness.

And here is the mercy hidden in it: sometimes we only recognise our own sin when we hear it named out loud in someone else's accusation. The brothers are about to protest their innocence — and in doing so, they will run straight into their real guilt.

God's Word does the same work in us. It names things plainly, and that naming stings. But conviction is not condemnation. The Spirit convicts so that we will run to Christ, where there is no condemnation left for us at all (Rom 8:1).

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. How do you respond when someone names a fault in you?
2. Can you tell the difference between the Spirit's conviction and the enemy's condemnation?
3. Where do you need to stop defending yourself and simply come to Christ?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, when Your Word names my sin, give me a soft heart instead of a defensive one. Thank You that conviction leads me to Jesus, where there is no condemnation. Amen.
